title: Evaluation of anti-smoking television advertising on tobacco control among urban community population in Chongqing, China
extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether a televised anti-smoking campaign influenced tobacco-related knowledge, attitudes, and self-reported behavioral intentions among urban community residents in Chongqing, China. The study focuses on the reach, recall, and perceived effects of a public health advertisement called “An Invisible Killer in the Office,” especially whether people who recognized the ad differed from those who did not in smoking-related beliefs and responses. Although the retrieval topic requested a secondary study on ChatGPT and academic writing, the provided text is clearly a different paper on tobacco-control media effects, with an exact DOI and journal metadata confirming the mismatch.

The intervention was a 25-second anti-smoking television advertisement adapted from a UK campaign and broadcast daily from 15 May to 15 June 2011 across 12 Chongqing TV channels in five time slots per day. The ad emphasized the dangers of secondhand smoke in an office setting and aimed to increase awareness and motivate smoking cessation. The evaluation used a post-campaign street-intercept cross-sectional survey, asking respondents whether they had seen the ad and measuring self-reported reactions such as whether the ad made them stop and think, felt relevant, provided new information, encouraged quitting, or prompted them to persuade others to stop smoking.

The population consisted of urban residents aged 18–45 in four randomly selected districts of Chongqing, Western China. A total of 1,265 respondents were included in analysis after exclusions; 238 reported seeing the advertisement. Data were collected face to face in public squares and university-area intercept sites, and outcomes were analyzed using descriptive statistics and logistic regression. The study was conducted in a community rather than educational setting, so no school-based population, classroom implementation, writing task, or academic assessment rubric applies.

The authors conclude that the advertisement had some positive self-reported effects, particularly among smokers: it increased concern about smoking harms and led some smokers to consider quitting. However, it did not produce clear differences in smoking-related knowledge and attitudes among non-smokers who had seen the ad versus those who had not. Gender, age, and smoking status were associated with some campaign responses. Overall, the paper suggests that this kind of TV advertisement may be more useful for targeting smokers than non-smokers, while also noting substantial methodological limitations such as reliance on post-campaign self-report, lack of baseline data, and limited generalizability.
